title: The experiment identifies the program: 1-4 chosen queries collapse 399-400 candidates, and correctness is only ever established on probes the choice never saw
the_theorem_that_replaces_the_earlier_gu: An observation identifies a hypothesis exactly as far as the candidates are behaviourally distinguishable on it: log2 of the number of behavioural classes it induces among the live candidates. Measured: the corpus case that fails `lis` splits 399 candidates into 399 classes (8.64 bits); the corpus case that fails `kth` splits 400 into 1 (0 bits). An uninformative observation is not weak experience, it is a badly chosen experiment.
the_architecture_this_implies: Not experience -> memory. Experiment -> identification. The object is a behaviour table (candidates x probes -> output); identification is set arithmetic; the next experiment is the probe that splits the survivors hardest. All of it computed from the program and the oracle, none of it stored, none of it trained.
what_the_failures_are_and_are_not: None of the three failures is an identification failure. `possible_change` loses every candidate on the first probe: the fix is not in the pool at the chosen site, so no number of queries can find it. `mergesort` and `next_permutation` stop with 3 and 2 survivors that no probe in the pool separates -- the pool is not discriminative enough, which is a property of the material, not of the evidence. `kth` converges to one candidate that is wrong on 7 of 14 held-out probes, at a site where the pool cannot express the fix at all.
the_rule_this_establishes: A capability claim is only as strong as its held-out agreement. "Identified" without held-out probes is a corpus artifact -- the same failure this tree has had to retract twice.
